screens.title: Assembly Language: Symbols, Labels, and Mnemonics
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll treat assembly language as a readable map of machine code. Assembly replaces raw binary with short mnemonics and symbolic names, making programs easier to write and reason about. You will learn the two main instruction forms in Hack — the A-instruction that sets the address register, and the C-instruction that carries out computations and jumps — and you’ll learn how labels and symbols let you name addresses and variables. We’ll also walk through how an assembler performs a two-pass process: first it records label addresses, then it translates each instruction into a 16-bit code. Along the way you’ll see concrete examples: predefined symbols like R0 and SCREEN, a simple program that adds two R A M cells and loops, and how variables are assigned memory starting at address sixteen. By the end, you should be able to read small Hack assembly programs, predict the assembler’s symbol table, and mentally map mnemonic instructions to machine-code patterns. Consider why symbolic names matter when code grows: debugging a label is easier than hunting a hard-coded address.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives guide how you will work with Hack assembly. First, you will be able to explain why assembly exists: it is a symbolic layer over machine language that reduces errors and improves readability. Second, you will describe the syntax of A-instructions, C-instructions, labels, and symbols so you can author correct programs. Third, you will translate small assembly programs into 16-bit machine code by using the assembler’s translation tables for comp, dest, and jump fields. Finally, you will explain the assembler’s two-pass process, so you understand how symbols are resolved and how variables are allocated starting at address sixteen. Each objective includes a concrete skill: reading an A-instruction like an address load, composing a C-instruction with a computation and optional jump, walking a program to build a symbol table, and producing the final binary output. These skills matter because they let you debug low-level programs, reason about memory layout, and understand the bridge between high-level languages and the machine.

screens.title: Skills & assessment targets
screens.narratorSegment: These learning objectives are practical. You will demonstrate competence by translating short programs, building a symbol table, and explaining why the assembler resolves symbols in two passes. For example, when you see a symbol like "i" in an A-instruction, you will decide whether it is a label previously recorded, a predefined name like R2, or a variable needing allocation. You will practice with the provided hands-on tasks: computing a maximum, summing integers in a loop, and counting negative values in a set of R A M cells. Each task requires writing commented assembly, constructing the symbol table, and producing the 16-bit binary output. Assessments will check that you correctly place labels at ROM addresses, allocate new variables starting at address 16, and translate C-instructions using the comp/dest/jump fields. A common misconception to watch for is assuming variable addresses are the same as label addresses — labels map ROM positions while variables map R A M addresses starting at 16. Keep that distinction clear as you practice.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Assessment Targets
Practical tasks
  • Max of two numbers: compare RAM[0] and RAM[1], store max in RAM[2].
  • Sum 1 to n: loop using a counter and accumulator, store in RAM[1].
  • Count negatives: check RAM[0]..RAM[9], store count in RAM[10].
Evaluation checklist
  • Label addresses recorded correctly by first pass.
  • Variables allocated starting at address 16.
  • C-instructions translated with correct comp/dest/jump bits.
Mnemonic reminder
Think: A-instruction sets an address, C-instruction computes and optionally jumps.
Common misconception
Labels define ROM addresses; variables map to RAM starting at 16. They are not interchangeable.

screens.title: Why Assembly Language?
screens.narratorSegment: Assembly language exists because writing raw binary is tedious and fragile. A single wrong bit can change an operation, and long machine-code numbers are hard to interpret. Assembly replaces those numbers with short mnemonics and labels so you can reason about program behavior. For example, instead of a 16-bit pattern you write a C-instruction like D=D+A. That tells you the computation directly: add the A register to D and store the result in D. Symbols like @LOOP or @i let you name addresses. Naming matters: when code changes, the assembler updates numeric addresses for you instead of forcing you to edit many hard-coded numbers. Assembly also enables self-documenting programs: a variable named sum tells future readers its role better than an address like 17. A frequent misconception is that assembly is only for experts; in fact, it’s the natural stepping stone between machine code and higher-level languages. Assembly gives complete control over registers and memory layout while remaining readable enough to debug. As you work with Hack assembly, practice translating short snippets by hand to internalize how mnemonics map to machine behavior.

keyIdea.title: Readable control over machine code
keyIdea.text: Assembly keeps the machine’s power while making programs human-manageable through mnemonics and symbols.

content.html:
Core Concept › Why Assembly
What assembly gives you
  • Human-readable mnemonics instead of raw 0s and 1s.
  • Symbolic addresses and labels that make code navigable.
  • Variables with meaningful names that document intent.
  • Portability of names: assembler resolves numeric addresses.
Analogy
Think of mnemonics as street names and labels as landmarks; the assembler maps them into numeric coordinates the machine understands.
Concrete example
// add R0 and R1, store in R2
@R0
D=M
@R1
D=D+M
@R2
M=D
This sequence directly states the programmer’s intent: fetch, add, and store. The assembler converts the mnemonic operations to bits.
Key Takeaway

Assembly reduces cognitive load: you work with names and computations, not raw binary patterns.

screens.title: A-instructions: Address and value loading
screens.narratorSegment: A-instructions are the simplest Hack assembly form. They begin with an at sign followed by either a non-negative decimal number or a symbol. When you write an at-signed number, the assembler produces a 16-bit instruction whose low fifteen bits hold that number and whose top bit is zero. Conceptually, the A-instruction loads the A register with either the literal number or the resolved address of a symbol. When the operand is a symbol, the assembler must decide whether it is predefined, a label, or a user variable — and that decision depends on the symbol table built by the assembler. For example, writing at sign R0 loads the address zero into A because R0 is predefined. Writing at sign LOOP loads the ROM address previously defined by a label named LOOP. A common mistake is to assume symbol names are translated immediately; instead, variable names are assigned addresses only during the second pass. Practice reading A-instructions aloud as “load address X into A” and then check whether X is numeric or needs resolution. This habit clarifies intent when you later translate to binary.

keyIdea.title: A-instruction = address loader
keyIdea.text: An A-instruction sets the A register to a number or to the address the assembler finds for a symbol.

content.html:
Definition › A-instructions
A-instruction form
Starts with an at sign followed by either a decimal number (0–32767) or a symbol. If number, A gets that value; if symbol, assembler resolves it to an address.
Examples
@21    // loads 21 into A
@R0    // predefined: loads address 0 into A
@LOOP  // symbol: address found in symbol table
Common mistake
Assuming a symbol is immediately a variable. If symbol is a label recorded during the first pass, it maps to a ROM address; if not, it may become a variable allocated at the next free RAM address starting at 16.
Translate to bits
A-instruction binary starts with a zero bit then fifteen bits representing the value. Practicing conversion by hand helps you verify assembler output.
Try this
Convert @2 to its 16-bit representation: zero plus fifteen-bit binary for 2.
Key Takeaway

A-instructions either embed a literal number or carry a symbol the assembler resolves into a numeric address.

screens.title: C-instructions: Computation, Destination, and Jump
screens.narratorSegment: C-instructions perform computations and optionally store results or jump. Their general format is dest equals comp semicolon jump, where either the dest or the jump part may be omitted. The comp field describes the computation — for example, D plus A, M minus one, or logical not of D. The dest field lists one or more targets to receive the computation’s result such as A, D, M or combinations like MD and AMD. The jump field holds a condition like greater-than or equal that controls program flow. When translated, the assembler uses reference tables to map comp, dest, and jump into the respective bit patterns of a 16-bit instruction. A common confusion is thinking dest controls what register is used as an input; it is only an output target. Practice by reading D=D+A as compute D plus A, then write result into D. Another useful habit is to check whether comp accesses M, which means memory at the address in A is read — that changes whether A must already contain a ROM or R A M address. End each translation by verifying both the computation bits and the correct dest and jump encodings.

keyIdea.title: C-instruction components
keyIdea.text: C-instructions combine a computation with optional output destinations and optional conditional jumps; each field maps to bits by lookup tables.

content.html:
Core Concept › C-instructions
Syntax: dest=comp;jump
comp
Computation expressions such as D+A, M-1, !D, 0.
dest
Targets: A, D, M or combinations like MD, AMD.
jump
Conditions: JGT, JEQ, JGE, JLT, JNE, JLE, JMP.
Example
D=A         // copy A into D
D=D+A       // add A to D, keep in D
M=D;JGT     // store D into memory at A, jump if result > 0
Quick checklist
  • Is comp referencing M? If so, A must point to the RAM address.
  • Dest lists outputs, not inputs.
  • Jump appears only if you want to change control flow.
Common mistake

Confusing dest with comp inputs leads to incorrect register usage. Read comp as the expression and dest as where to store the result.

screens.title: Labels: Landmarks in ROM
screens.narratorSegment: Labels are pseudo-instructions that mark ROM addresses without generating machine code. When you place a label like open-parenthesis LOOP close-parenthesis, you declare that the next real instruction’s ROM address should be associated with the name LOOP. This lets the program reference LOOP later with an A-instruction like at sign LOOP, even if the reference appears before the label itself. That forward reference is possible only because the assembler performs an initial scan to record all labels and their ROM addresses. Labels differ from variables: labels name ROM positions and never consume R A M slots, while variables refer to R A M addresses starting at sixteen. A common misconception is to treat labels as runtime values; they are purely assembly-time names that guide address resolution. Labels also help readability: name places you jump to with meaningful identifiers like END, LOOP, or CHECK_NEGATIVE. When you build a symbol table by hand, list each label with the ROM address it defines — that becomes the authoritative mapping the assembler uses during translation. Labels: Landmarks in ROM means a label records the rom address of the next instruction; it does not emit machine code and is used for symbolic jumps and references.. In practical terms, how (label_name) defines rom addresses and supports forward references. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Labels define ROM addresses
keyIdea.text: A label records the ROM address of the next instruction; it does not emit machine code and is used for symbolic jumps and references.

content.html:
Definition › Labels
Label form
(LABEL_NAME) records the ROM address of the next instruction. It is not translated into machine code but used by the assembler to resolve symbol references.
Example
(END)
@END
0;JMP
Here, END maps to the ROM address of the unconditional jump instruction that follows.
Label vs variable
Labels map ROM addresses for control flow; variables allocate RAM addresses (starting at 16). Confusing them can break both address resolution and memory layout.
Pro tip

When labeling loops, pick descriptive names so the symbol table acts as a readable legend for your program flow.

screens.title: Predefined Symbols and User Symbols
screens.narratorSegment: Hack defines a small set of predefined symbols that map to fixed R A M addresses. The names R0 through R15 map to addresses zero through fifteen and are convenient register aliases. Special symbols like SCREEN and KBD map to memory-mapped IO regions at large addresses, and SP, LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT map to commonly used stack and segment locations. User-defined symbols fall into two categories: labels, which name ROM addresses, and variables, which refer to R A M addresses allocated by the assembler starting at address sixteen. When the assembler encounters a symbol during translation, it first checks if it is predefined. If not, it checks whether that name was recorded as a label in the first pass. If still unresolved, the symbol is treated as a variable and assigned the next free R A M address. One misconception is assuming all programmer names are variables; labels behave differently and occupy no R A M slot. Keeping predefined, label, and variable namespaces clear helps avoid address collisions and mistaken assumptions about memory use. Predefined Symbols and User Symbols means symbols may be predefined, labels, or user variables; the assembler resolves them in that order and assigns variables from ram address 16 upward.. In practical terms, how the assembler treats r0–r15, screen, kbd, and program-defined names. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Symbol categories
keyIdea.text: Symbols may be predefined, labels, or user variables; the assembler resolves them in that order and assigns variables from RAM address 16 upward.

content.html:
Core Concept › Symbols
Predefined symbols
R0–R15 → addresses 0–15
SCREEN → 16384, KBD → 24576
These are immediate mappings the assembler already knows.
Labels
(NAME) records the ROM address of the next instruction; used for branching and references.
Labels are resolved during the assembler's first pass.
Variables
Any non-predefined, non-label symbol becomes a variable assigned from address 16 up.
Variables occupy RAM on translation; be mindful of address space limits.
Key Takeaway

Symbols follow a clear resolution order: predefined → label → variable; variables are assigned starting at RAM address 16.

screens.title: Variable allocation and RAM layout
screens.narratorSegment: Variables in Hack assembly are allocated by the assembler during translation. Addresses zero through fifteen are reserved for predefined registers R0 through R15. Because of this reservation, the assembler assigns the first user variable to R A M address sixteen, then increments for each new variable encountered. Practically, that means if you write at sign i and i is not predefined or a label, the assembler will map i to address 16 the first time it sees it, then to 17 for the next new name, and so on. This policy preserves the low addresses for common register-like uses and decouples variable naming from fixed machine addresses. A common question is what happens when many variables are used; the chapter notes that using more than about 240 variables could reach addresses that collide with the stack area beginning at 256. That constraint arises from the limited R A M space on the Hack platform. When you design assembly programs, minimize the number of persistent variables and prefer loops and the stack for larger data structures. As you practice, write out a small symbol table and simulate allocation to become fluent with the mapping.

keyIdea.title: RAM allocation starts at 16
keyIdea.text: User variables receive RAM addresses beginning at 16; this preserves addresses 0–15 for predefined registers.

content.html:
Process Flow › Variable allocation
Allocation rule
First free RAM address for user variables is 16. Each new variable name gets the next free address during the assembler’s second pass.
Example allocation
First new symbol: i  → 16
Next new symbol: sum → 17
Next: temp       → 18
Why this matters
Reserved registers at low addresses support fast temporary storage and standard conventions used by compilers and the VM translation stages.
Warning

Allocating too many variables may approach the stack area starting at address 256 on the Hack machine; manage variable use carefully.

screens.title: The Assembler's Two-Pass Process
screens.narratorSegment: The assembler translates assembly into 16-bit machine code via a two-pass approach. On the first pass, it scans every line to record labels and the ROM addresses they represent. Because labels do not produce machine code, counting addresses during this pass requires ignoring label lines and incrementing the address counter only for real instructions. After the first pass you have a symbol table that maps label names to ROM addresses, which enables forward references. The second pass translates each A-instruction and C-instruction into binary. During this pass the assembler resolves symbols: if a symbol is predefined, it uses that address; if it was recorded as a label, it uses the label’s address; otherwise it treats the symbol as a variable and assigns a R A M address starting at sixteen. This two-stage method ensures that references to labels that appear before their definitions still work. A common misconception is that translation happens in one sweep; that would fail for forward references. Practice building a symbol table by hand on the first pass to solidify the process. The Assembler's Two-Pass Process means pass one records label-to-rom mappings; pass two translates instructions and assigns ram addresses for new variables.. In practical terms, first pass: collect labels. second pass: translate and assign variables.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Pass one records label-to-ROM mappings; pass two translates instructions and assigns RAM addresses for new variables.

content.html:
Process Flow › Two-pass assembler
Pass One — Label collection
Scan lines, ignore label pseudo-ops for ROM counting, and record each label with the address of the next real instruction.
Checklist
  • Increment ROM address only for A- and C-instructions.
  • Record label names with the current ROM address.
  • Build initial symbol table entries from labels.
Pass Two — Translate & allocate
Translate each instruction, resolve symbols using predefined and recorded labels, and allocate new variables starting at address 16 when needed.
Key Takeaway

Two passes allow forward references and a clean separation between label discovery and instruction encoding.

screens.title: Symbol Resolution Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: Symbol resolution follows a strict priority. When the assembler encounters a symbol, it first checks the predefined table: names like R0–R15, SCREEN, and KBD are already mapped to fixed addresses. If the symbol is not predefined, the assembler checks the label entries recorded during the first pass. If a match is found, the symbol maps to that ROM address. If the symbol is neither predefined nor a recorded label, it is treated as a variable: the assembler assigns the next free R A M address starting at sixteen and records that in the symbol table so subsequent uses of the same name reuse the assigned address. This deterministic approach ensures consistent mapping per assembly run and supports forward references that appear before labels are defined. One pitfall students face is assuming case-insensitive names or automatic reuse of names across programs. The assembler’s symbol table is local to the assembled program and exact string matches are required. Practice by walking through sample code, listing each symbol decision and the resulting table entry. Symbol Resolution Strategy means the assembler resolves symbols by checking predefined names first, then labels, then assigning variables from ram address 16 upward when needed.. In practical terms, how the assembler determines whether a name is predefined, a label, or a variable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Concept › Symbol resolution
Resolution steps
  1. Check predefined symbol table (R0–R15, SCREEN, KBD, SP, LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT).
  2. If not predefined, check labels recorded in pass one.
  3. If still unresolved, allocate a new RAM address starting at 16 and add it to the table as a variable.
This predictable ordering prevents ambiguity between labels and variables and supports forward label references.
Example decision
If symbol LOOP appears and labels include LOOP, use that address; if not and LOOP is new, assign it RAM address 16.
Check your understanding

When you see @i in pass two, explain how the assembler decides i's numeric address.

screens.title: Instruction Translation: From Mnemonic to 16-bit
screens.narratorSegment: Translating a C-instruction requires looking up three fields in reference tables and assembling their bits into a 16-bit instruction header that begins with ones. The comp field encodes the computation bits; comp patterns differ depending on whether memory M or register A is referenced. The dest field encodes which targets receive the result, using three bits for A, D, and M. The jump field encodes the jump condition using three bits as well. When assembling, you first determine the comp bits for the requested computation, then set the dest bits by checking which of A, D, and M appear on the left side, and finally set the jump bits according to the condition mnemonic. A typical translation example is D=D+M;JGT which computes D plus memory and stores in D, then jumps if the result is greater than zero. Practicing manual translation trains you to cross-check each lookup and catch mistakes like using the A-based comp pattern when the expression references M. Building fluency with these tables is the core mechanical skill of assembly translation. Instruction Translation: From Mnemonic to 16-bit means c-instructions are assembled by concatenating comp bits, dest bits, and jump bits according to lookup tables; errors usually come from wrong field selection.. In practical terms, how comp, dest, and jump fields map to binary patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: C-instructions are assembled by concatenating comp bits, dest bits, and jump bits according to lookup tables; errors usually come from wrong field selection.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough › Translating C-instructions
Step-by-step
  1. Determine comp expression and choose the correct comp bit pattern (watch for M vs A).
  2. Set dest bits: three-bit mask for A, D, M targets.
  3. Set jump bits according to the condition mnemonic; no jump = 000.
  4. Concatenate fields into the 16-bit C-instruction pattern.
Example conversion (conceptual): D=D+M;JGT converts comp for D+M, dest bits for D, and jump bits for greater-than, producing the final binary instruction.
Concrete hint
If comp includes M, choose the comp pattern with the a-bit set to indicate memory access. If comp includes only A or constants, use the a-bit cleared patterns.
Key Takeaway

Carefully pick comp patterns and dest/jump bits; most translation errors come from choosing the wrong comp variant or dest mask.

screens.title: Example Walkthrough: Add and Loop Program
screens.narratorSegment: Let’s walk through the example program that computes R A M[2] = R A M[0] + R A M[1] and then loops forever. The assembly snippet uses predefined names R0, R1, and R2 for addresses zero, one, and two. The instructions load the contents of R0 into D, add the contents of R1, and store the result into R2. After those data instructions, a label named END marks the loop start and an A-instruction references END to form an unconditional jump. Translating this by hand, first note predefined symbols: R0→0, R1→1, R2→2. There are no user variables, only a label END defined at the ROM address following the store instruction. When you convert each instruction to binary, A-instructions become zero plus the fifteen-bit address, and each C-instruction uses comp/dest/jump tables to produce the correct one-and-one patterns. For example, the unconditional jump instruction 0;JMP translates into the C-instruction pattern whose comp bits encode the constant zero and whose jump bits encode unconditional. A good check is to produce the full symbol table listing R0, R1, R2, END→6, and validate that @END becomes the binary for address six. That verification proves your translation is correct.

keyIdea.title: Full example validation
keyIdea.text: Translating an end-to-end example shows predefined symbols, label addresses, and final binary output all align when the symbol table is correct.

content.html:
Example › Program walkthrough
Assembly program
// Compute RAM[2] = RAM[0] + RAM[1]
@R0
D=M
@R1
D=D+M
@R2
M=D

// Infinite loop
(END)
@END
0;JMP
Symbol table
R0 → 0 R1 → 1 R2 → 2 END → 6
Selected translations
@R0 → @0 → 0000000000000000 D=M → 1111110000010000 @END → @6 → 0000000000000110 0;JMP → 1110101010000111
Key Takeaway

Verify translation by checking the symbol table then converting each mnemonic to its binary representation; predefined names simplify the mapping.

screens.title: Key Concepts

screens.title: Quick Reference
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three quick rules in mind as you write and translate Hack assembly. Rule one: treat labels as ROM landmarks — they map to the address of the next instruction and do not consume R A M. Rule two: variables are R A M entries allocated from address sixteen upward; predefined symbols occupy addresses zero through fifteen and special IO addresses. Rule three: always perform symbol resolution in two stages: discover labels first, then translate instructions and assign variables. These rules let you reason about forward references, avoid address collisions, and debug translations by checking the symbol table first. When you run into an unexpected binary output, inspect whether symbols were resolved correctly and whether you accidentally mixed label and variable usage. content.html:
Quick Reference › Cheat sheet
Labels
(NAME) → ROM address of next instruction. Used for jumps and references.
Predefined & variables
R0–R15 reserved; variables begin at 16; SCREEN and KBD map to fixed IO addresses.
Two-pass rule
Pass one: record labels. Pass two: translate instructions and assign variable addresses.
Final thought
When you translate programs, always validate the symbol table before trusting the binary output; that is where most errors hide.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll treat assembly language as a readable map of machine code. Assembly replaces raw binary with short mnemonics and symbolic names, making programs easier to write and reason about. You will learn the two main instruction forms in Hack — the A-instruction that sets the address register, and the C-instruction that carries out computations and jumps — and you’ll learn how labels and symbols let you name addresses and variables. We’ll also walk through how an assembler performs a two-pass process: first it records label addresses, then it translates each instruction into a 16-bit code. Along the way you’ll see concrete examples: predefined symbols like R0 and SCREEN, a simple program that adds two R A M cells and loops, and how variables are assigned memory starting at address sixteen. By the end, you should be able to read small Hack assembly programs, predict the assembler’s symbol table, and mentally map mnemonic instructions to machine-code patterns. Consider why symbolic names matter when code grows: debugging a label is easier than hunting a hard-coded address.

These objectives guide how you will work with Hack assembly. First, you will be able to explain why assembly exists: it is a symbolic layer over machine language that reduces errors and improves readability. Second, you will describe the syntax of A-instructions, C-instructions, labels, and symbols so you can author correct programs. Third, you will translate small assembly programs into 16-bit machine code by using the assembler’s translation tables for comp, dest, and jump fields. Finally, you will explain the assembler’s two-pass process, so you understand how symbols are resolved and how variables are allocated starting at address sixteen. Each objective includes a concrete skill: reading an A-instruction like an address load, composing a C-instruction with a computation and optional jump, walking a program to build a symbol table, and producing the final binary output. These skills matter because they let you debug low-level programs, reason about memory layout, and understand the bridge between high-level languages and the machine.

These learning objectives are practical. You will demonstrate competence by translating short programs, building a symbol table, and explaining why the assembler resolves symbols in two passes. For example, when you see a symbol like "i" in an A-instruction, you will decide whether it is a label previously recorded, a predefined name like R2, or a variable needing allocation. You will practice with the provided hands-on tasks: computing a maximum, summing integers in a loop, and counting negative values in a set of R A M cells. Each task requires writing commented assembly, constructing the symbol table, and producing the 16-bit binary output. Assessments will check that you correctly place labels at ROM addresses, allocate new variables starting at address 16, and translate C-instructions using the comp/dest/jump fields. A common misconception to watch for is assuming variable addresses are the same as label addresses — labels map ROM positions while variables map R A M addresses starting at 16. Keep that distinction clear as you practice.

Assembly language exists because writing raw binary is tedious and fragile. A single wrong bit can change an operation, and long machine-code numbers are hard to interpret. Assembly replaces those numbers with short mnemonics and labels so you can reason about program behavior. For example, instead of a 16-bit pattern you write a C-instruction like D=D+A. That tells you the computation directly: add the A register to D and store the result in D. Symbols like @LOOP or @i let you name addresses. Naming matters: when code changes, the assembler updates numeric addresses for you instead of forcing you to edit many hard-coded numbers. Assembly also enables self-documenting programs: a variable named sum tells future readers its role better than an address like 17. A frequent misconception is that assembly is only for experts; in fact, it’s the natural stepping stone between machine code and higher-level languages. Assembly gives complete control over registers and memory layout while remaining readable enough to debug. As you work with Hack assembly, practice translating short snippets by hand to internalize how mnemonics map to machine behavior.

A-instructions are the simplest Hack assembly form. They begin with an at sign followed by either a non-negative decimal number or a symbol. When you write an at-signed number, the assembler produces a 16-bit instruction whose low fifteen bits hold that number and whose top bit is zero. Conceptually, the A-instruction loads the A register with either the literal number or the resolved address of a symbol. When the operand is a symbol, the assembler must decide whether it is predefined, a label, or a user variable — and that decision depends on the symbol table built by the assembler. For example, writing at sign R0 loads the address zero into A because R0 is predefined. Writing at sign LOOP loads the ROM address previously defined by a label named LOOP. A common mistake is to assume symbol names are translated immediately; instead, variable names are assigned addresses only during the second pass. Practice reading A-instructions aloud as “load address X into A” and then check whether X is numeric or needs resolution. This habit clarifies intent when you later translate to binary.

C-instructions perform computations and optionally store results or jump. Their general format is dest equals comp semicolon jump, where either the dest or the jump part may be omitted. The comp field describes the computation — for example, D plus A, M minus one, or logical not of D. The dest field lists one or more targets to receive the computation’s result such as A, D, M or combinations like MD and AMD. The jump field holds a condition like greater-than or equal that controls program flow. When translated, the assembler uses reference tables to map comp, dest, and jump into the respective bit patterns of a 16-bit instruction. A common confusion is thinking dest controls what register is used as an input; it is only an output target. Practice by reading D=D+A as compute D plus A, then write result into D. Another useful habit is to check whether comp accesses M, which means memory at the address in A is read — that changes whether A must already contain a ROM or R A M address. End each translation by verifying both the computation bits and the correct dest and jump encodings.

Labels are pseudo-instructions that mark ROM addresses without generating machine code. When you place a label like open-parenthesis LOOP close-parenthesis, you declare that the next real instruction’s ROM address should be associated with the name LOOP. This lets the program reference LOOP later with an A-instruction like at sign LOOP, even if the reference appears before the label itself. That forward reference is possible only because the assembler performs an initial scan to record all labels and their ROM addresses. Labels differ from variables: labels name ROM positions and never consume R A M slots, while variables refer to R A M addresses starting at sixteen. A common misconception is to treat labels as runtime values; they are purely assembly-time names that guide address resolution. Labels also help readability: name places you jump to with meaningful identifiers like END, LOOP, or CHECK_NEGATIVE. When you build a symbol table by hand, list each label with the ROM address it defines — that becomes the authoritative mapping the assembler uses during translation. Labels: Landmarks in ROM means a label records the rom address of the next instruction; it does not emit machine code and is used for symbolic jumps and references.. In practical terms, how (label_name) defines rom addresses and supports forward references. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Hack defines a small set of predefined symbols that map to fixed R A M addresses. The names R0 through R15 map to addresses zero through fifteen and are convenient register aliases. Special symbols like SCREEN and KBD map to memory-mapped IO regions at large addresses, and SP, LCL, ARG, THIS, THAT map to commonly used stack and segment locations. User-defined symbols fall into two categories: labels, which name ROM addresses, and variables, which refer to R A M addresses allocated by the assembler starting at address sixteen. When the assembler encounters a symbol during translation, it first checks if it is predefined. If not, it checks whether that name was recorded as a label in the first pass. If still unresolved, the symbol is treated as a variable and assigned the next free R A M address. One misconception is assuming all programmer names are variables; labels behave differently and occupy no R A M slot. Keeping predefined, label, and variable namespaces clear helps avoid address collisions and mistaken assumptions about memory use. Predefined Symbols and User Symbols means symbols may be predefined, labels, or user variables; the assembler resolves them in that order and assigns variables from ram address 16 upward.. In practical terms, how the assembler treats r0–r15, screen, kbd, and program-defined names. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Variables in Hack assembly are allocated by the assembler during translation. Addresses zero through fifteen are reserved for predefined registers R0 through R15. Because of this reservation, the assembler assigns the first user variable to R A M address sixteen, then increments for each new variable encountered. Practically, that means if you write at sign i and i is not predefined or a label, the assembler will map i to address 16 the first time it sees it, then to 17 for the next new name, and so on. This policy preserves the low addresses for common register-like uses and decouples variable naming from fixed machine addresses. A common question is what happens when many variables are used; the chapter notes that using more than about 240 variables could reach addresses that collide with the stack area beginning at 256. That constraint arises from the limited R A M space on the Hack platform. When you design assembly programs, minimize the number of persistent variables and prefer loops and the stack for larger data structures. As you practice, write out a small symbol table and simulate allocation to become fluent with the mapping.

The assembler translates assembly into 16-bit machine code via a two-pass approach. On the first pass, it scans every line to record labels and the ROM addresses they represent. Because labels do not produce machine code, counting addresses during this pass requires ignoring label lines and incrementing the address counter only for real instructions. After the first pass you have a symbol table that maps label names to ROM addresses, which enables forward references. The second pass translates each A-instruction and C-instruction into binary. During this pass the assembler resolves symbols: if a symbol is predefined, it uses that address; if it was recorded as a label, it uses the label’s address; otherwise it treats the symbol as a variable and assigns a R A M address starting at sixteen. This two-stage method ensures that references to labels that appear before their definitions still work. A common misconception is that translation happens in one sweep; that would fail for forward references. Practice building a symbol table by hand on the first pass to solidify the process. The Assembler's Two-Pass Process means pass one records label-to-rom mappings; pass two translates instructions and assigns ram addresses for new variables.. In practical terms, first pass: collect labels. second pass: translate and assign variables.. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let’s walk through the example program that computes R A M[2] = R A M[0] + R A M[1] and then loops forever. The assembly snippet uses predefined names R0, R1, and R2 for addresses zero, one, and two. The instructions load the contents of R0 into D, add the contents of R1, and store the result into R2. After those data instructions, a label named END marks the loop start and an A-instruction references END to form an unconditional jump. First, assembly language provides a symbolic, readable form of machine code using mnemonics and symbols, which makes programs easier to write, understand, and debug. Second, the Hack syntax has two instruction types: A-instructions that load addresses or values into A, and C-instructions that perform computations, store results, and control jumps through dest, comp, and jump fields. Third, labels, predefined symbols, and user variables are handled distinctly: labels define ROM addresses, predefined names map to fixed R A M addresses, and variables are assigned R A M from address sixteen upward. Keep these distinctions clear when you build symbol tables and translate programs. Keep three quick rules in mind as you write and translate Hack assembly. Rule one: treat labels as ROM landmarks — they map to the address of the next instruction and do not consume R A M. Rule two: variables are R A M entries allocated from address sixteen upward; predefined symbols occupy addresses zero through fifteen and special IO addresses. Rule three: always perform symbol resolution in two stages: discover labels first, then translate instructions and assign variables. These rules let you reason about forward references, avoid address collisions, and debug translations by checking the symbol table first. When you run into an unexpected binary output, inspect whether symbols were resolved correctly and whether you accidentally mixed label and variable usage.
